newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Stals upbeat on rand as bull run continues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stals upbeat on rand as bull run continues.

text.p: South Africa's Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Wednesday he saw scope for a "very stable" rand in 1997, buoyed by a sharply better balance of payments position.
Stals told Reuters the currency could decline by less than the inflation differentials between South Africa and its major trading partners after overshooting in 1996.

After a dismal 1996, South Africa's currency and bond markets have been in buoyant mood this year. The rand hit its best level on the dollar since early December on Wednesday, gaining more than two cents to trade below 4.63, despite the greenback's strength against other currencies.
Last year's depreciation of the rand had, at least in the short-term, created an under-valued currency, Stals said by telephone from Pretoria.
"The New Year seems to have started with a new sense of optimism and a feeling that 1997 will see some consolidation, some stabilisation and some improvement in the underlying conditions," he said.
"Seven or eight percent will be the inflation differential but we've already discounted that last year in the over-reaction, so the rand can be very stable this year."

Dealers and analysts said there was a growing belief that a slowing economy will see the trade balance improve sharply this year, rebuilding the low reserves that have made the rand a target for speculative attacks.
Stals agreed, predicting the current account of the balance of payments would improve sharply in 1997.
"If last year's deficit was about 10 billion rand ($2.2 billion), it could be half of that this year -- about four to five billion rand," he said.

Stals said he expected economic growth to slow to around two percent in 1997 from some three percent in 1996 while consumer price inflation should average less than 10 percent, against the 9.2 percent recorded in November.
This year's rash of Eurorand bond issues was also a sign of growing confidence in the South African currency and the economic outlook.
"It is encouraging that European investors are prepared to take new positions in rand," Stals said.
However, Stals put a slight dampener on market euphoria, cautioning he would keep a tight rein on monetary policy in order to rein in excessive money supply and credit growth.

Commenting on South Africa's high money market shortage of more than 10 billion rand a day, which is keeping short-term interest rates high, Stals said the liquidity squeeze helped the authorities keep bank credit extension in check.
"It gives us a much greater influence on bank credit extension and the money supply. We are in no hurry to try and reduce the shortage," he said.
Economists said investors were not looking to the government to give further clarifiation on issues such as privatisation, government spending and foreign exchange controls in the coming months.
Substantive statements on these issues are expected from President Nelson Mandela's opening of parliament on February 7 and in Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's budget on March 12.
